## What you will learn

After this tutorial, you should be able to:

- state the different questions answered by power flow (PF) and state estimation (SE);
- distinguish their specified inputs, equations, and outputs;
- explain why a PF Jacobian is usually square while an SE measurement Jacobian is usually rectangular;
- distinguish PF solvability from SE observability; and
- reproduce both calculations on the same small network.

The [Newton--Raphson power-flow tutorial](newton-raphson-power-flow.qmd) and the [weighted least-squares state-estimation tutorial](weighted-least-squares-state-estimation.qmd) derive the two methods in detail; here the emphasis is their relationship and the boundary between them.

## 1. The short answer

**Power flow:** given a network model, bus types, and user specified injections or voltages, what steady-state voltage satisfies the power equations?

**State estimation:** given a network model and a redundant set of noisy measurements, what voltage (grid state variables) are most likely to produce measurements?

@tbl-pfse-comparison compares the two methods.


| Aspect | Power flow calculation | State estimation |
|---|---|---|
| Main purpose | Predict or study a steady operating point | Reconstruct the present operating state from data |
| Typical inputs | Topology, parameters, bus types, scheduled $P$ and $Q$, controlled $|V|$ | Topology, parameters, meter values, pseudo-measurements, uncertainty model |
| Equation form | Balance equations $\mathbf g(\mathbf v,\mathbf s_{\mathrm{spec}})=\mathbf 0$ | Measurement model $\mathbf z=\mathbf h(\mathbf v)+\mathbf e$ |
| Number of equations | Usually square after bus types and reference are set | Usually overdetermined, $m>n$, to provide redundancy |
| Treatment of inconsistent data | Specifications define the case; inconsistency may prevent a solution | Residuals are reconciled according to measurement weights |
| Key structural question | Is the operating point locally solvable? | Is the state observable from the available measurements? |
| Typical diagnostics | Mismatch norm, iteration count, limits, Jacobian conditioning | Objective, residuals, bad-data tests, rank, state uncertainty |
| Typical use | Planning, contingency studies, optimisation studies, simulation | Control-room monitoring, topology/error detection, downstream applications |

: Power flow and state estimation comparison {#tbl-pfse-comparison}

::: {.callout-important}
SE is not simply “power flow with measured injections.” An estimator can combine injection measurements with branch flows, voltage magnitudes, currents, and phasors, seeking a state that best fits all retained evidence rather than enforcing every measured quantity as an exact balance specification.
:::

## 2. Power flow: enforce a specified operating case

Let $\mathbf v$ denote the unknown voltage-state vector of unfixed voltage angles and magnitudes, and let $\mathbf s_{\mathrm{spec}}$ collect the specified operating-case quantities such as scheduled injections and controlled voltage magnitudes. PF solves

$$
\mathbf g(\mathbf v,\mathbf s_{\mathrm{spec}})=\mathbf0.
$$ {#eq-pfse-pf-model}

For an AC formulation, $\mathbf g$ contains selected active- and reactive-power mismatches. Bus types decide which quantities are specified and which are unknown. Newton's method linearises the square retained system,

$$
\mathbf J_k\,\Delta\mathbf v_k
=-\mathbf g(\mathbf v_k,\mathbf s_{\mathrm{spec}}),
\qquad
\mathbf J_k
=\left.\frac{\partial\mathbf g}{\partial\mathbf v}\right|_{\mathbf v_k}.
$$ {#eq-pfse-pf-newton}

A converged solution is a **model-based operating point** consistent with the chosen network model and specifications---not proof that a physical system actually occupied that state. Forecast errors, an incorrect topology, or inaccurate parameters can all make a converged case differ from reality.

The local mathematical question is whether the retained PF Jacobian is nonsingular and adequately conditioned. The [power-flow Jacobian tutorial](power-flow-jacobian-invertibility.qmd) explains why reference choices, operating stress, and voltage-collapse boundaries matter.

## 3. State estimation: reconcile uncertain evidence

Let $\mathbf z$ contain $m$ measurements and let $\mathbf h(\mathbf v)$ predict those measurements from a candidate voltage state. The static measurement model is

$$
\mathbf z=\mathbf h(\mathbf v)+\mathbf e,
\qquad
\mathbb E[\mathbf e]=\mathbf0,
\qquad
\operatorname{cov}(\mathbf e)=\mathbf R.
$$ {#eq-pfse-se-model}

Weighted least squares (WLS) chooses

$$
\widehat{\mathbf v}
=\underset{\mathbf v}{\arg\min}\;
[\mathbf z-\mathbf h(\mathbf v)]^{\mathsf T}
\mathbf R^{-1}
[\mathbf z-\mathbf h(\mathbf v)].
$$ {#eq-pfse-wls-objective}

At a nonlinear Gauss--Newton iteration, the $m\times n$ measurement Jacobian

$$
\mathbf H_k
=\left.\frac{\partial\mathbf h}{\partial\mathbf v}\right|_{\mathbf v_k}
$$ {#eq-pfse-measurement-jacobian}

maps a state correction to changes in all predicted measurements. The WLS step uses the $n\times n$ gain matrix $\mathbf H_k^{\mathsf T}\mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf H_k$. Unlike the PF Jacobian, $\mathbf H_k$ is normally rectangular because redundancy is valuable.

After fixing the voltage-angle reference, local observability requires $\mathbf H_k$ to have full column rank. Redundancy then leaves post-fit residuals that can reveal inconsistency. Full rank alone does not guarantee accurate estimates: covariance errors, bad data, parameter errors, and poor conditioning still matter [@monticelli1999stateestimation].

## 4. The same three-bus network, two calculations

Consider the balanced three-bus AC network in @fig-pfse-three-bus-ac. The lines retain both resistance and reactance, so the calculations involve complex voltages, active and reactive power, voltage-magnitude variation, and transmission losses. The series impedances are

$$
z_{12}=0.02+\mathrm j0.06,
\qquad
z_{13}=0.08+\mathrm j0.24,
\qquad
z_{23}=0.06+\mathrm j0.18
\quad\text{p.u.}
$$ {#eq-pfse-ac-impedances}

![The meshed three-bus AC network used for both calculations. Bus 1 is the slack bus, bus 2 is a PV bus, and bus 3 is a PQ bus. Branch labels give the per-unit series impedances.](figures/generated/three-bus-power-flow-single-line.svg){#fig-pfse-three-bus-ac fig-align="center" width="100%"}

With $\mathbf Y$ assembled from the three series admittances, the calculated complex-power injection at bus $i$ is

$$
S_i(\mathbf V)=P_i+\mathrm jQ_i
=V_i\left(\sum_{k=1}^{3}Y_{ik}V_k\right)^*.
$$ {#eq-pfse-ac-injection}

For a series-only branch from bus $i$ to bus $j$, the sending-end flow used below is

$$
S_{ij}(\mathbf V)
=P_{ij}+\mathrm jQ_{ij}
=V_i\left(\frac{V_i-V_j}{z_{ij}}\right)^*.
$$ {#eq-pfse-ac-branch-flow}

### 4.1 PF calculation

The operating-case specifications are

| Bus | Type | Specified quantities |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | Slack | $|V_1|=1.04$ p.u., $\theta_1=0$ |
| 2 | PV | $P_2=0.50$ p.u., $|V_2|=1.01$ p.u. |
| 3 | PQ | $P_3=-0.60$ p.u., $Q_3=-0.25$ p.u. |

: AC power-flow specifications {#tbl-pfse-ac-specifications}

Negative $P_3$ and $Q_3$ denote consumption. The PF state contains the quantities not fixed by the bus specifications,

$$
\mathbf x_{\mathrm{PF}}
=\begin{bmatrix}\theta_2&\theta_3&|V_3|\end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf T},
$$ {#eq-pfse-ac-pf-state}

and Newton's method solves the nonlinear square system

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
P_2(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{PF}})\\
P_3(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{PF}})\\
Q_3(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{PF}})
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0.50\\-0.60\\-0.25
\end{bmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-pfse-ac-pf-system}

The slack-bus powers and $Q_2$ are outputs of PF rather than additional specifications.

### 4.2 SE calculation

SE uses the same admittance matrix but a different state and different inputs: only the angle reference $\theta_1=0$ is fixed. The estimator state is

$$
\mathbf x_{\mathrm{SE}}
=\begin{bmatrix}
\theta_2&\theta_3&|V_1|&|V_2|&|V_3|
\end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf T}.
$$ {#eq-pfse-ac-se-state}

The redundant measurement vector combines all three voltage magnitudes, the active and reactive injections at buses 2 and 3, and the sending-end active and reactive flows on branches 1--2 and 2--3:

$$
\mathbf h(\mathbf x)=
\begin{bmatrix}
|V_1|&|V_2|&|V_3|&P_2&Q_2&P_3&Q_3&P_{12}&Q_{12}&P_{23}&Q_{23}
\end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf T}.
$$ {#eq-pfse-ac-measurement-function}

For this controlled experiment, the converged AC PF result supplies the reference state in the estimator's coordinates,

$$
\mathbf x_{\mathrm{ref}}=
\begin{bmatrix}
\theta_{2,\mathrm{PF}}&\theta_{3,\mathrm{PF}}&
|V_{1,\mathrm{PF}}|&|V_{2,\mathrm{PF}}|&|V_{3,\mathrm{PF}}|
\end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf T}.
$$ {#eq-pfse-ac-reference-state}

The ideal measurement values and the values passed to SE are therefore

$$
\mathbf z_{\mathrm{ideal}}=\mathbf h(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{ref}}),
\qquad
\mathbf z_{\mathrm{SE}}=\mathbf z_{\mathrm{ideal}}+\mathbf e.
$$ {#eq-pfse-ac-synthetic-measurements}

The fixed errors in the code emulate imperfect meters while keeping every render reproducible. They are added only after PF has produced the reference voltages and the measurement functions have been evaluated---never to the PF specifications. Nonlinear WLS then repeatedly evaluates $\mathbf h$ and its $11\times5$ Jacobian.

```{python}
#| label: lst-pfse-side-by-side
#| code-summary: "Solve nonlinear AC PF and WLS SE on the same network"

import numpy as np

np.set_printoptions(precision=6, suppress=True)

slack_voltage = 1.04
pv_voltage = 1.01
lines = [
    (0, 1, 0.02 + 0.06j),
    (0, 2, 0.08 + 0.24j),
    (1, 2, 0.06 + 0.18j),
]

y_bus = np.zeros((3, 3), dtype=complex)
for from_bus, to_bus, impedance in lines:
    admittance = 1.0 / impedance
    y_bus[from_bus, from_bus] += admittance
    y_bus[to_bus, to_bus] += admittance
    y_bus[from_bus, to_bus] -= admittance
    y_bus[to_bus, from_bus] -= admittance


def numerical_jacobian(function, state):
    """Return a central-difference Jacobian."""
    jacobian = np.empty((function(state).size, state.size))
    for column in range(state.size):
        step = 1e-6 * max(1.0, abs(state[column]))
        forward = state.copy()
        backward = state.copy()
        forward[column] += step
        backward[column] -= step
        jacobian[:, column] = (function(forward) - function(backward)) / (2.0 * step)
    return jacobian


def bus_power(voltage):
    """Return positive complex-power injections at all buses."""
    return voltage * (y_bus @ voltage).conjugate()


def pf_voltage(state):
    """Map [theta2, theta3, |V3|] to the PF voltage phasors."""
    angle = np.array([0.0, state[0], state[1]])
    magnitude = np.array([slack_voltage, pv_voltage, state[2]])
    return magnitude * np.exp(1j * angle)


def retained_pf_injections(state):
    power = bus_power(pf_voltage(state))
    return np.array([power.real[1], power.real[2], power.imag[2]])


# PF: three exact specifications determine three unknown state variables.
specified = np.array([0.50, -0.60, -0.25])
x_pf = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0])
for pf_iteration in range(12):
    pf_residual = specified - retained_pf_injections(x_pf)
    if np.linalg.norm(pf_residual, ord=np.inf) < 1e-10:
        break
    pf_jacobian = numerical_jacobian(retained_pf_injections, x_pf)
    x_pf += np.linalg.solve(pf_jacobian, pf_residual)
else:
    raise RuntimeError("AC power flow did not converge")

voltage_pf = pf_voltage(x_pf)
power_pf = bus_power(voltage_pf)


def se_voltage(state):
    """Map [theta2, theta3, |V1|, |V2|, |V3|] to voltage phasors."""
    angle = np.array([0.0, state[0], state[1]])
    return state[2:] * np.exp(1j * angle)


def branch_power(voltage, from_bus, to_bus, impedance):
    current = (voltage[from_bus] - voltage[to_bus]) / impedance
    return voltage[from_bus] * current.conjugate()


def measurement_function(state):
    voltage = se_voltage(state)
    injection = bus_power(voltage)
    flow_12 = branch_power(voltage, *lines[0])
    flow_23 = branch_power(voltage, *lines[2])
    return np.array(
        [
            *np.abs(voltage),
            injection[1].real,
            injection[1].imag,
            injection[2].real,
            injection[2].imag,
            flow_12.real,
            flow_12.imag,
            flow_23.real,
            flow_23.imag,
        ]
    )


# SE: ideal measurements come from the converged PF voltage state.
x_reference = np.array(
    [
        np.angle(voltage_pf[1]),
        np.angle(voltage_pf[2]),
        *np.abs(voltage_pf),
    ]
)
measurement_names = np.array(
    [
        "|V1|",
        "|V2|",
        "|V3|",
        "P2",
        "Q2",
        "P3",
        "Q3",
        "P12",
        "Q12",
        "P23",
        "Q23",
    ]
)
sigma = np.array(
    [0.004, 0.004, 0.004, 0.015, 0.015, 0.015, 0.015, 0.012, 0.012, 0.012, 0.012]
)
fixed_error = np.array(
    [0.002, -0.003, 0.001, 0.008, -0.006, -0.009, 0.007, 0.006, -0.005, -0.004, 0.006]
)
z_ideal = measurement_function(x_reference)
z_measured = z_ideal + fixed_error

# Nonlinear WLS from a flat start using a whitened Gauss--Newton step.
x_se = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0])
for se_iteration in range(20):
    h = measurement_function(x_se)
    H = numerical_jacobian(measurement_function, x_se)
    correction, _, _, _ = np.linalg.lstsq(
        H / sigma[:, None], (z_measured - h) / sigma, rcond=None
    )
    x_se += correction
    if np.linalg.norm(correction, ord=np.inf) < 1e-10:
        break
else:
    raise RuntimeError("AC state estimation did not converge")

H = numerical_jacobian(measurement_function, x_se)
se_prediction = measurement_function(x_se)
se_residual = z_measured - se_prediction
se_rank = np.linalg.matrix_rank(H / sigma[:, None])

print("PF iterations =", pf_iteration)
print("maximum PF residual =", np.linalg.norm(pf_residual, ord=np.inf))
print("PF voltage magnitudes p.u. =", np.abs(voltage_pf))
print("PF voltage angles deg =", np.rad2deg(np.angle(voltage_pf)))
print("PF injections [P1, P2, P3] p.u. =", power_pf.real)
print("PF injections [Q1, Q2, Q3] p.u. =", power_pf.imag)
print("SE iterations =", se_iteration)
print("SE state [theta2, theta3, |V1|, |V2|, |V3|] =", x_se)
print("SE error relative to PF reference =", x_se - x_reference)
print("measurement-Jacobian rank =", se_rank)
print("\nmeasurement   PF-derived  measured    SE prediction  residual")
for name, ideal, measured, predicted, residual in zip(
    measurement_names, z_ideal, z_measured, se_prediction, se_residual
):
    print(
        f"{name:11s} {ideal:10.6f} {measured:10.6f} "
        f"{predicted:14.6f} {residual:10.6f}"
    )
```

The PF residual confirms that its three retained specifications are satisfied to numerical tolerance, and its solved voltage phasors determine every ideal value in the measurement table. The SE state is close but not identical to that PF reference because no voltage state can reproduce all 11 perturbed values exactly; WLS accepts residuals and distributes them according to the stated standard deviations.

Similar outputs do not imply identical tasks: PF uses three exact operating-case **specifications** to calculate the reference voltages, while SE uses 11 uncertain **observations** derived from those voltages to estimate five state variables.

::: {.callout-note}
This is the full nonlinear AC solution of the stated balanced, positive-sequence, series-impedance model, not a DC approximation. A more detailed model can add transformer taps, shunts, line charging, phase connections, and unbalance without changing the PF--SE distinction.
:::

## 5. How the methods work together

PF and SE are often consecutive rather than competing tools:

1. SE converts raw telemetry into a coherent present-state model.
2. Operators use that estimated state to initialise contingency PF studies, security analysis, and optimisation.
3. In method development, PF can generate a known synthetic state from which ideal measurements are calculated.
4. Noise, bad data, and model errors can then be applied before SE is run and compared with that known state.

The last two steps form the verification workflow developed in [A Typical Verification Workflow for State Estimation Methods](state-estimation-verification-workflow.qmd). Synthetic verification is valuable because the reference state is known exactly, but using the same model on both sides tests algorithmic recovery under controlled assumptions---not every source of real-world error.

## 6. Takeaways

- PF maps operating specifications to a network state by enforcing balance equations.
- SE maps uncertain, redundant measurements to a best-fit network state and residual diagnostics.
- PF solvability concerns a square balance Jacobian; SE observability concerns the column rank of a generally rectangular measurement Jacobian.
- A PF solution can supply controlled synthetic truth for testing an estimator, provided the validation also addresses noise, bad data, model mismatch, and stressed conditions.
